title: Three watches (Berakhot 3a)
hook: the night has three watches, and in each the Talmud pictures God grieving for the exile
tomorrow: how did King David know when it was midnight?

segments.voice: Yesterday, masechet: one tractate, in order, opening with when evening begins. Rabbi Eliezer said: until the end of the first watch. So what's a watch?

Two in the morning, phone face down, and the house makes its night sounds: the fridge, a dog somewhere, a car going by. Berakhot's next page divides the night exactly that way, by what you hear. And it says that in every part of the night, someone else is awake too.
screen: `2 A.M. THE NIGHT SOUNDS.` → `THE NIGHT, TOLD BY EAR.` → `WHO ELSE IS AWAKE?`

segments.voice: The night has three watches, says Rabbi Eliezer, and each has a sign. In the first, the donkey brays. In the second, dogs bark. In the third, a baby nurses at its mother's breast, and a wife talks quietly with her husband. You can tell the hour by ear. Then the page adds something startling. In the name of Rav it says: in each watch, God sits and roars like a lion, grieving. Woe to the children, for whose sake I destroyed My house, burned My Temple, and sent them into exile among the nations. The verse behind it is from Jeremiah: the LORD roars from on high. So in this picture, God is the one awake at two in the morning, missing children who are far away. Not a judge on a bench. A parent at the window. The same page doesn't leave it there. When people gather in their synagogues and study halls and answer, may His great name be blessed, God shakes His head and says: happy is the king who is praised like this in his house. Grief and comfort, side by side. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud tells time by a donkey, a dog and a baby, and then says God keeps those watches too. So being awake in the night, thinking of someone far away, isn't only a failure to sleep. On this page, it's what God does.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who's far away tonight, across town or across an ocean. Picture the hour where they are and what they might be hearing: a dog, traffic, a kettle. Keep them company in your mind for the whole sit.

howItsDone: Many Jews say the bedtime Shema before sleep, and some keep a custom called Tikkun Chatzot, rising around midnight to mourn the destruction of the Temple.

chat.meaning: In Berakhot 3a God keeps all three watches, grieving for children far away. Lying awake for someone you love fits that page.
